title: Chaos Engineering: Breaking Things on Purpose
intro: Netflix's Chaos Monkey made the idea famous: if failures will happen anyway, cause small ones deliberately, at a time you choose, to prove the system survives them. Every experiment has a hypothesis, a small blast radius, a way to abort, and someone watching. Start in staging.

steps.prompt: Hypothesis: cart tolerates 200ms of extra latency to redis. On the staging host cart-stg-01, add 200ms ±50ms of delay to all traffic leaving eth0.
expected_commands: sudo tc qdisc add dev eth0 root netem delay 200ms 50ms
tc qdisc add dev eth0 root netem delay 200ms 50ms
steps.fake_output: (no output: every packet leaving eth0 is delayed 150-250ms)
steps.explanation: Network latency is injected at the kernel level.
steps.why: tc netem simulates slow, lossy, or jittery networks with no application change, which is exactly what happens during a cloud network degradation or a cross-region failover. Keep a second terminal ready with the removal command before you start.

steps.prompt: Confirm the rule is active on eth0.
expected_commands: sudo tc qdisc show dev eth0
steps.fake_output: qdisc netem 8001: root refcnt 2 limit 1000 delay 200ms  50ms
steps.why: Always verify the fault is really injected. An experiment that 'passed' because the fault never applied gives false confidence.

steps.prompt: Observe: cart's p99 latency jumped from 40ms to 3s, and some requests time out. The hypothesis was wrong. Abort the experiment: remove the netem rule from eth0.
expected_commands: sudo tc qdisc del dev eth0 root
tc qdisc del dev eth0 root
steps.why: A failed hypothesis is a successful experiment: you found, in staging, that cart makes about 15 sequential redis calls per request, so 200ms of latency multiplies into seconds. Fix that (batch the calls, set timeouts) before a real network blip finds it in production.

steps.prompt: Next experiment, on Kubernetes: kill one random cart pod in shop-staging with Chaos Mesh. Apply podchaos-kill-cart.yaml.
steps.explanation: Chaos Mesh will kill one pod matching app=cart.
steps.why: Chaos Mesh (and LitmusChaos) run experiments as Kubernetes resources: pod kills, network faults, CPU and memory stress, clock skew. Because the experiment is YAML, it can be reviewed, versioned, scheduled, and run as a regular 'game day' test.

steps.prompt: Check the experiment's status in shop-staging.
steps.fake_output:
NAME            ACTION     DURATION   AGE
kill-one-cart   pod-kill              40s
(events: Killed pod cart-5c7d9f8b6-h2j4k; a replacement was Ready after 6s; error rate unchanged)
steps.explanation: One pod was killed; the replacement was ready in 6s and users saw nothing.
steps.why: That's the hypothesis confirmed: multiple replicas, a readiness probe, and a PodDisruptionBudget mean a lost pod is invisible. Run the same experiment regularly, since a later change (a slow startup, one replica) can silently break this resilience.

steps.prompt: Clean up: delete the PodChaos kill-one-cart in shop-staging.
steps.why: Leftover chaos resources keep injecting faults, which is an easy way to create a confusing incident a week later. Every experiment ends with explicit cleanup and a short write-up of what was learned.
